job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Tara Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can give me both the public version and the private one. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in the first term of a master's in data science at Millbrook, a conversion course for people whose first degree was something else, though mine was software engineering. I wake up in a shared house with three flatmates, do lectures or labs until about three, then pull a shift at the campus café on Tuesdays and Thursdays. The rest is applications and a lot of tea.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What was your final project last year?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A booking app for our local food bank, so volunteers can sign up for shifts instead of using a messy group chat. It worked, and the food bank manager, Dilys, still uses it. I passed my degree with an average mark, and I had no internship, so Dilys's reference is the best thing on my CV.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it matches what I've seen. I use a chatbot now and then to explain an error message, and it saves ten minutes, nothing more. I'd tell friends not to panic and not to get excited either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the worry isn't AI at all. It's that I'm average on paper and the grad schemes want firsts. I owe around 11,000 and my parents can help in a pinch, but they're a nurse and a teacher, so a pinch is a small thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's and put my food bank app on a proper portfolio page. I'd send out five applications a week, mostly to local councils and health trusts, which hire people for software that actually helps. I'd keep the café shifts for rent money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, mostly. There's a low hum of pressure from the debt, but I know the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why councils and health trusts rather than big tech?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want my work to be something Dilys-type people use, and those places hire graduates with average marks if they show real projects. Big firms filter on grades before they even look. I'd rather be useful to a food bank than invisible at a firm that rejects me by spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does the 11,000 sit on your list of worries?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Near the top, but it's the kind of debt that only bites when I earn over a limit. The bigger thing is feeling like I'm already behind friends who got offers. I try not to compare, and I do it anyway.

say: AI is **useful**, but only a modest time saver so far.
I'd tell friends to **stay calm**, neither panic nor celebrate.
think: The real problem is my **average degree**, not AI.
I owe about **11,000** and my parents' help is small.
do: **Build** a portfolio page around the food bank booking app.
Send **five applications** a week to councils and health trusts.
Keep the **café shifts** on Tuesdays and Thursdays for rent.
feel: **Steady**, with a low hum of pressure from debt.
S0.quote: I'd rather be useful to a food bank than invisible at a firm that rejects me by spreadsheet.
fieldNote: Steady adapter: she has a plan and sticks to it.
Her **purpose** is public-service software, which shapes where she applies.
Compares herself to friends with offers and admits it.

steps.text: Put the food bank booking app on a portfolio page
Send five applications a week to councils and health trusts
Keep the Tuesday and Thursday café shifts for rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where my generation gets squeezed. The coding and testing jobs that used to be a first rung are the ones that tools do now. I'd post that employers need to be honest about it and unions need to get involved early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think about half the junior roles I'd apply for get merged into fewer, more senior ones. My data course could help, because someone has to understand what the tools produce. I'm not sure it's enough for an average graduate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the tools properly, not just now and then. I'd pick one data project a month and finish it with AI help, and write down what it got wrong. I'd also ask my mum's teaching union whether they run anything for new members' children, since networks matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but alert. I feel like a person watching the tide come in and looking for higher ground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does writing down what it got wrong do for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes me the person who checks. Anyone can paste a prompt, but if I can say 'this model confuses dates and ignores missing values' then I'm worth hiring. The skill I'm building is being the person who can tell when the machine is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who worries you most at work in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people a year or two behind me, and the ones who didn't get a data course. And honestly my flatmate Mo, who's on a pure coding path. He's brilliant, but junior coding is exactly what gets taken first.

say: Employers should be **honest** about which junior roles disappear.
Unions need to **act** early, before the cuts start, not after people are gone.
think: Many junior roles get merged into fewer **senior** ones.
My data course helps only if I become the one who **checks**.
do: Use AI tools **properly** on one data project each month.
Keep a **log** of what the tools got wrong.
Ask my mother's **union** about networks for members' children.
feel: **Anxious** but alert, looking for higher ground.
S1.quote: The skill I'm building is being the person who can tell when the machine is wrong.
fieldNote: Steady adopter: moves once the change is proven and visible.
Turns the threat into a **niche**: checking the machine's work.
Worries about a flatmate on a pure coding path.

steps.text: Finish one data project a month using AI help
Keep a log of model mistakes to show in interviews
Ask my mother's union about mentoring for graduates
Join the graduate branch of a tech workers' union

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is not a plan, it's a crash. I'd tell everyone I know to talk to their MP, and to ask who pays when entry-level work vanishes. I'd be loud about it online, which isn't like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be frightened. I've a master's that finishes in 2027 and AGI the year after. My student loan would be ready to start and the jobs would be shrinking at the same moment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the café shifts' small treats and put every spare pound into savings. I'd move back to my parents' spare room after the course. I'd apply anywhere, including jobs near people like care homes, since robots take longer for hands-on work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared and a bit numb. I think I'd go through the motions for a month before it sank in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be loud online, which isn't like you. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Long posts, honestly, and tagging my MP. I'd also go to a rally if one existed. I'm not good at shouting, but when everyone's future is on one clock, staying quiet feels like agreeing to the deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm sorry the degree plan might not pay off and that I'm coming home. Mum would put the kettle on and say we'll sort it out. She's a teacher, she thinks everything's a lesson plan, and I'd let her.

say: Two years is **not a plan**; I'd lobby my MP.
I'd ask who **pays** when entry-level work vanishes.
think: My master's and the loan start just as jobs **shrink**.
I'd be **frightened**, though I'd hide it at first.
do: **Save** every spare pound instead of small treats.
Move back into my parents' **spare room** after the course.
Apply for **care** and public-service jobs, which need people longest.
feel: **Scared** and numb, going through the motions for a month.
S2.quote: when everyone's future is on one clock, staying quiet feels like agreeing to the deadline.
fieldNote: Her steadiness turns into **action** online and with her MP.
Chooses people-facing work as the safer shelter.
Keeps a family plan: home to her parents' **spare room**.

steps.text: Put every spare pound into a savings account
Write to the MP and share posts on graduate jobs
Move back to the parents' spare room after the course
Apply for care home and public service technology roles

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a window and we should use it. I'd talk about retraining funds and say governments tend to move when there's a deadline everyone can see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd get a first job in the next year, probably in data or public sector software, and then I'd have about three years of experience before AGI lands. That's something. I could save most of my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a first job by the end of next year and live on half the pay. I'd pay down the 11,000 quickly while I can. And I'd learn one more area, maybe health data, since hospitals will need people who can judge what systems say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful and nervous together. The window is real, but it doesn't close gently.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why half the pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the early years are the only years I can be sure about. If the working years are limited, I'd rather spend them clearing debt than buying things I'll be paying for later. A fresh start without debt is worth more to me than a nicer flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the hospital idea come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad's a nurse, and he complains that the new software gives him alerts that make no sense. Someone who understands both the data and the ward would be valuable. It would be a bridge between my world and his.

say: Five years is a **window**, and we should use it well.
Governments move when there is a **visible deadline**.
think: I could get a **first job** and three years of experience.
I can save most of my **pay** if I stay careful.
do: Land a **first job** in data or public sector software.
Live on **half** my pay and clear the 11,000 debt.
Learn **health data**, since hospitals will need people to judge systems.
feel: **Hopeful** and nervous at once about the window.
S3.quote: If the working years are limited, I'd rather spend them clearing debt than buying things I'll be paying for later.
fieldNote: Moves from fear to **planning** when a window exists.
Father's work as a nurse gives her a **niche** idea.
Debt-first mindset: freedom matters more than comfort.

steps.text: Land a first job in data or public sector software by next year
Live on half of the pay and clear the 11,000 loan
Take a short health data course on evenings and weekends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to rebuild the whole system if we start early. I'd tell friends that the useful thing to do is learn and organise now, and not wait for the date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm fairly calm. I'd be 34 and could have a decade of real experience, savings, maybe a flat deposit. By then I could be a person who understands both data and the people it affects.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a decent job, then work toward a senior data role over five years. I'd keep a small fund for retraining and add a course every year or two. And I'd stay in a union, because no one person can negotiate with a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. There's still a little knot, but it's the normal kind that comes with any long future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's in the knot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether the people who need help most will get it. I can plan for my own future, but I can't plan for the food bank, and that's where the real trouble would land. Dilys already turns people away some weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the long timeline make you complacent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't think so. Ten years is long enough to drift, and I know that. That's why I'd set a yearly review, like a tiny annual check of what I've learnt and what's changed.

say: Ten years is enough to **rebuild** the system if we start now.
Learn and **organise** now; don't wait for the date.
think: By 34 I could have **experience**, savings and a deposit.
I can plan for myself but not for **vulnerable** people.
do: Take a decent **job** and aim for a senior data role.
Add a **course** every year or two from a small fund.
Stay in a **union** to bargain collectively.
feel: **Mostly calm**, with a small knot about the vulnerable.
S4.quote: I can plan for my own future, but I can't plan for the food bank, and that's where the real trouble would land.
fieldNote: Her worry is outward-facing: the **food bank** and its users.
Sets a yearly self-review so a long timeline does not make her drift.

steps.text: Take a decent data job and aim for a senior role in five years
Add one short course a year from a small retraining fund
Stay in the union and go to yearly meetings
Hold an annual review of skills and savings each January

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because the pieces don't fit together in time. What would help is a clear public plan, with retraining pay and a guarantee that new graduates are counted in it, and not forgotten.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe that average graduates exist and matter. Everyone talks about the brilliant ones and the ones who lose out, but the people in the middle are the ones holding up the services.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about the brilliant ones and the ones who lose out, but the people in the middle are the ones holding up the services.
portrait: Tara is 24, studying a **data science** master's after a pass degree in software engineering.
She lives in a shared house in **Millbrook** and works Tuesday and Thursday shifts at a café.
Progressive, with parents in a **nursing** and a teaching job, she trusts unions and public plans.
Steady and practical, she uses AI **now and then** and plans to become the person who checks it.
Her mood moves between **uneasy** and anxious, and she turns fear into a plan.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most, since the loan and the job cuts would arrive together.
whatWouldHelp: A clear **public plan** with retraining pay that counts new graduates.
